papers.title_in_file: Parameter Setting Heuristics Make the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm Suitable for the Early Fault-Tolerant Era
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, sections 3 to 6 (discussion); references skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: An invited short review by JPMorganChase authors on how QAOA parameters can be set cheaply, so that QAOA can be run on early fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not expect broadly applicable speedups from QAOA experiments on early fault-tolerant hardware without significant advances in error correction, and that currently proposed surface-code architectures are unlikely to be competitive in time to solution.
assertions.anchor: Section 1 Introduction, p.1
quotes: we do not expect broadly applicable speedups from such experiments in absence of significant advances in error correction.
currently proposed quantum architectures like those based on the surface code [4] are unlikely to be competitive in terms of
assertions.certainty_reason: An expectation stated by the authors in the introduction, not backed by a result in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors work for a bank; this is a cautious statement from an industry group about its own algorithm family.

assertions.value: The authors state that QAOA parameters are known to be instance-independent when the QAOA depth is kept constant, so parameters optimized for small instances of a problem class can be used on larger instances with little or no reoptimization.
assertions.anchor: Section 1 Introduction, p.1
quotes: QAOA parameters are known to be instance-independent if the QAOA depth (i.e. the number of alternating operators) is kept constant
optimize the parameters for small instances from a given problem class once and use these parameters on larger instances with little or no reoptimization
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes this to prior work (its references 5 and 10 to 12); it is a cited result.

assertions.value: The authors report, from a cited protocol, that fine-tuning of QAOA parameters can be done with a small shot budget of at most 10k shots, and that the trust-region optimizers COBYLA and BOBYQA perform best in that shot-limited setting.
assertions.anchor: Section 4 End-to-end parameter setting protocol, p.4
quotes: Since fine-tuning can be accomplished with a small (≤ 10k) shot budget, this end-to-end protocol is directly applicable to the shot-constrained EFTQC setting.
The benchmark shows that trust-region optimizers with a simple internal model, namely COBYLA [54] (linear model) and BOBYQA [55] (quadratic model) perform best in this setting.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical benchmark result from the cited Ref. [30], summarized here.

assertions.value: The authors state that the evidence of a QAOA speedup over classical state of the art has so far been demonstrated only on small instances of up to 40 qubits in classical simulation, and that those results focus on small problems because they come mainly from classical simulation.
assertions.anchor: Section 1 p.1 and Section 5.1 Evaluating the evidence of QAOA speedup, p.4
quotes: which so far have only been demonstrated on small (≤ 40 qubits) instances in classical simulation [11, 61].
they focus on small problems. This is due to the results obtained primarily by classical simulation of deep circuits
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about the limits of other groups' cited results (Refs. 11, 46, 61), not a limit of this paper's own setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The speedup evidence rests on extrapolated scaling fits from small simulated instances; no hardware run is reported.

papers.title_in_file: Learning Fourier series with parametrized quantum circuits
papers.version_note: The file is arXiv 2209.10345 version 3 (21 May 2025), filed under a 2022 folder name; the title and content match the record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, prior work, start of results (Sec. IV A), discussion and outlook (Sec. V); appendices only skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A numerical study that defines a learning-capability measure for parametrized quantum circuit ansatze by how well they fit truncated Fourier series, and compares layered and dissipative ansatze.

assertions.value: The authors report that parametrized quantum circuits exist that provide all Fourier coefficients of a given degree yet differ in how well they fit different Fourier functions, and that among such layered ansatze the one with two entanglement layers fits degree 6 Fourier functions on average much better than the others.
assertions.anchor: Section IV A (Fig. 5), p.6; Section V, p.9
quotes: The learning capability experiments reveal that PQCs exist, which provide all Fourier coefficients for the respective degree, but differ in their ability to fit different Fourier functions
determining the learning capability reveals that the last ansatz, with two entanglement layers, fits Fourier functions of degree 6 on average much better than the other
assertions.certainty_reason: A numerical result from one study on simulated circuits.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in their setup, two entanglement layers in each trainable unitary give good learning capability for degree six Fourier functions and three entanglement layers for degree 12.
assertions.anchor: Section V Discussion and outlook, p.9
quotes: Our results show that two (respectively, three) entanglement layers in each W yield good learning capabilities for degree six (respectively, 12) functions.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical design guideline from numerical experiments.

assertions.value: The authors report that a data reupload technique turned out to be necessary for dissipative quantum neural network ansatze to learn the Fourier functions, and that having more hidden than input qubits led to better learning capability.
assertions.anchor: Section V Discussion and outlook, p.9
quotes: a data reupload technique, inspired by the reupload technique for layered PQCs, turned out to be necessary.
having more hidden than input qubits leads to better learning capabilities
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the assumption that performance on learning Fourier series carries over to general quantum machine learning tasks may not hold universally, and that all experiments use one-dimensional classical data with a fixed RX input encoding.
assertions.anchor: Section V Discussion and outlook, p.9-10
quotes: we emphasize that this assumption about the correlation between performance on Fourier series and general QML tasks, of course, may not hold universally.
In this work, we do not change the input encoding gate and use RX for one-dimensional classical data in all experiments.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their own study in Section V.
assertions.reader_inference: The guidelines come from a regression task on synthetic Fourier targets, not from a classification task on real data.

papers.title_in_file: On Optimizing Hyperparameters for Quantum Neural Networks
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, discussion, threats to validity and conclusion; results sections 5.1 to 5.8 skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: An empirical simulation study of which hyperparameters matter for Qiskit quantum neural networks on four classical tabular classification datasets, with and without noise.

assertions.value: The authors report that the optimizer was the most crucial hyperparameter to set for their quantum neural networks, and that Nelder-Mead consistently led to underperforming configurations independently of the other hyperparameters.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.9 Further analysis, p.10
quotes: One of the most prevalent patterns we discover is that the optimizer is the most crucial hyperparameter to set.
Using Nelder-Mead in our experiments consistently led to underperforming configurations, independently of any other hyperparameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study on four datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report that the exact entangling strategy had a negligible effect on model performance in their setting.
assertions.anchor: Section 1 Introduction (p.2) and Section 6 Discussion, p.10
quotes: The exact entangling strategy has a negligible effect on the performance of the model in our setting.
We find that the entanglement strategy has a negligible effect on the performance of the model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical null result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in contrast to a conjecture from earlier work, their additional experiments found that the beta distribution itself does not necessarily lead to better initial points, since a normal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation mostly gave no significant differences.
assertions.anchor: Section 7 Conclusion and future work, p.11
quotes: in contrast to the conjecture from [27], we found in additional experiments that the beta distribution itself does not necessarily lead to better initial points
Indeed, we mostly found no significant differences when initializing using a normal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation as the beta distribution
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical post-hoc result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results could vary with other datasets or with the whole dataset, because training samples were limited, and that what happens when the experiments are scaled from tens to hundreds or thousands of qubits is an open research question.
assertions.anchor: Section 6.1 Threats to validity, p.11
quotes: While the experiments on the four datasets allowed us to draw valuable conclusions, the results could vary with different ones.
As we had to limit the training samples, the results could vary when rerunning the experiments with the whole dataset.
It remains an open research question what happens when the experiments are scaled from tens to hundreds or thousands of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors list these as limits of their own study in Section 6.1.

papers.version_note: The file is arXiv 2304.08226 version 2 (19 Sep 2024), filed under a 2023 folder name; the title and content match the record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction (Sec. 1.1), Sec. 6.2.6 discussion, Sec. 6.3 comparison and start of Sec. 7; the algebra of Sections 3 and 4 and the appendices were not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: A classical machine learning paper that builds SO(3)-equivariant tensor networks and uses them as compressed polynomial machine-learning interatomic potentials for molecules and alloys.

assertions.value: The authors state that they develop a formalism for rank-efficient equivariant tensor networks that remain invariant under actions of SO(3) upon contraction, and that key tensor-network algorithms carry over to the equivariant case.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, p.1
quotes: In this work we develop a formalism for rank-efficient equivariant tensor networks (ETNs), i.e., tensor networks that remain invariant under actions of SO(3) upon contraction.
All the key algorithms of tensor networks like orthogonalization of cores and DMRG-based algorithms carry over to our equivariant case.
assertions.certainty_reason: An abstract-level statement of the paper's contribution; the derivations were not checked in this pass.
assertions.reader_inference: The topic is interatomic potentials in materials science; it is a tensor-network method, not a quantum-hardware method.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the MoNbTaVW high-entropy alloy dataset an ETN potential with a maximum angular momentum of only 1 achieves accuracy comparable to three Gaussian approximation potentials, and that the best ETN potential has the same energy error as the best of those potentials with a lower force error.
assertions.anchor: Section 6.3 Comparison with non-polynomial MLIPs and Table 3, p.23-24
quotes: Interestingly, an ETN potential with a maximum angular momentum of only 1 (ETN2) achieves a comparable accuracy to that of the three GAPs (Table 3).
The energy error for the best ETN potential (ETN3) is the same as for the best GAP (trGAP), while the force error is lower
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result on one dataset. The GAP errors in Table 3 are read off figures in other papers, so the comparison is indirect.

assertions.value: The authors state that converging ETN potentials on molecules with the python BFGS solver is difficult, in particular with higher body-order, and that the alternating least-squares solvers still need to be implemented, so a comparison for molecules is postponed to future work.
assertions.anchor: Section 6.3, p.23
quotes: we have found in Section 6.2.2 that converging ETN potentials on molecules with the python BFGS solver is difficult, in particular for ETN potentials with higher body-order.

While we have shown in Section 4 that alternating least-squares solvers are in principle stable for ETNs, they still need to be implemented and we thus postpone a comparison for molecules to future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state a limit of their own method in Section 6.3.

papers.title_in_file: Q-MAML: Quantum Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning for Variational Quantum Algorithms
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, related work, experiment setting, results, discussion and conclusion; the appendix was not read.
papers.what_it_is: A hybrid method in which a classical neural network (the Learner) is meta-trained to output initial parameters for a parametrized quantum circuit, tested in simulation on Heisenberg XYZ and molecule Hamiltonians.

assertions.value: The authors report that initializing a parametrized quantum circuit with the output of their Learner network (Q-MAML) gave faster convergence, and so lower quantum resource use, than the other initialization methods compared.
assertions.anchor: Results, p.4-5
quotes: Our framework features a classical neural network, called Learner, which interacts with a PQC using the output of Learner as an initial parameter.
The result implies that when initialized with Q-MAML, PQC can converge faster and therefore requires lower quantum resources compared to other methods.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the authors themselves word it as 'implies'. Figures, not tables, carry the numbers.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is against uniform and Gaussian initialization only.

assertions.value: The authors state that they test on Heisenberg Hamiltonians at 12 and 20 qubits and molecule Hamiltonians at 10 and 14 qubits, and that a separate parametrized circuit is trained for each task in the adaptation phase.
assertions.anchor: Experiment setting and Results, Figures 3 and 4, p.4-5
quotes: (a) Heisenberg 12 qubits (b) Heisenberg 20 qubits (c) Molecule 10 qubits (d) Molecule 14 qubits Figure 3: Training trajectory of Learner with different Hamiltonian dataset.
It should be noted that, unlike training of the Learner, separate PQC is used and trained per task.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup (Results section and Figure 3 caption).
assertions.reader_inference: No result on real hardware is reported in the parts read.

assertions.value: The authors infer from gradient norm trends that Q-MAML initial points lie in regions of moderate gradient norm closer to the optimum, and they write that this observation needs further discussion.
assertions.anchor: Discussion: How the Learner affects gradient norms, and A new perspective on barren plateaus, p.5-6
quotes: Although this observation needs further discussion, we can assume that the Learner provides better initial
Through observation, we can imply that the initialization point provided by Q-MAML is located in space with a moderate gradient norm, which is closer to the optimal value.
assertions.certainty_reason: An interpretation by the authors, hedged in their own wording, drawn from gradient-norm plots.
assertions.reader_inference: The conclusion says Q-MAML circumvents barren plateaus, but the evidence read is gradient-norm plots at 10 to 20 qubits; no direct barren-plateau test is described.

papers.title_in_file: How to Build a Quantum Supercomputer: Scaling from Hundreds to Millions of Qubits
papers.version_note: The file is arXiv 2411.10406 version 4 (8 Sep 2026). Its title differs from the file name (Scaling Challenges and Opportunities), which names an earlier version; same paper.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Section I introduction (first part), and Section VIII concluding remarks; the 400-page-scale body (hardware, resource estimates, hybrid stack, p-computers) was not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: A long multi-author review and position paper on scaling superconducting-qubit fault-tolerant quantum computers, with resource estimates for chemistry and materials applications.

assertions.value: The authors report that ground-state energy estimation of p-benzyne and FeMoCo at chemical accuracy requires hundreds of millions of physical qubits and a minimum of 1.4 years with current hardware quality, and that the runtime can be reduced to approximately four months and the qubit count to tens of millions with significantly improved hardware targets.
assertions.anchor: Section VIII Concluding remarks, p.60 (end of paper)
quotes: one requires hundreds of millions of physical qubits and a minimum of 1.4 years to run with current hardware quality
The runtime can be reduced to approximately four months and the qubit count to tens of millions if the hardware quality is significantly improved to our proposed targets.
assertions.certainty_reason: A model-based resource estimate that depends on the authors' assumed surface-code architecture and baseline hardware; not a measurement.
assertions.reader_inference: Several authors are from hardware and vendor organizations (HPE, Quantum Machines, NVIDIA, Qolab) that may benefit from the proposed architecture.

assertions.value: The authors state that they focus on superconducting qubits for digital gate-based fault-tolerant quantum computing, and that their discussion of scaling challenges does not necessarily apply to quantum annealers based on superconducting qubits.
assertions.anchor: Section I Introduction, p.2
quotes: we focus on superconducting qubits, in the context of digital (gate-based) fault-tolerant quantum computing.
Our discussion of scaling challenges and opportunities does not necessarily apply to quantum annealers based on superconducting qubits [15].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its scope in the Section I introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that evaluating any proposal for a utility-scale quantum computer, including theirs, is a challenging task spanning use cases, device architecture and the full range of computational methods, and that their work focuses primarily on the second criterion, an initial understanding of the size, scale and cost of a quantum supercomputer.
assertions.anchor: Section VIII Concluding remarks, p.60
quotes: Evaluating any proposal for a utility-scale quantum computer, including the vision we present here, is thus a challenging task involving answering questions spanning domain-specific use cases, device architecture and integration, and the full range of computational methods.
This work focuses primarily on the second criterion, providing an initial holistic understanding of the size, scale, and cost of a quantum supercomputer and identifying key challenges.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their own work in Section VIII.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not claim to show that no cheaper classical method exists for these tasks (the third criterion).

assertions.value: The authors report that their sensitivity analysis showed that improving the gate fidelities would improve the exponential error suppression of surface codes significantly more than reducing SPAM errors or protecting idling qubits.
assertions.anchor: Section VIII Concluding remarks, p.60 (analysis in Section III C)
quotes: Our sensitivity analysis revealed that improving the gate fidelities would improve the exponential error suppression of surface codes significantly more than reducing SPAM errors or protecting idling qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulation-based result under the authors' error model for superconducting qubits.

papers.title_in_file: Comparative Analysis of Quantum and Classical Support Vector Classifiers for Software Bug Prediction: An Exploratory Study
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, dataset table and RQ3 setup, RQ1 results (Table 2), threats to validity, related work and conclusion; later result tables were not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: An exploratory simulation study comparing quantum support vector classifiers (QSVC, PQSVC) with a classical SVC for detecting buggy commits in 14 open-source software projects.

assertions.value: The authors report that on short-term activity frame datasets with approximately 350 to 500 training instances, QSVC consistently either matched or closely rivalled the classical SVC on the remaining subject systems, while PQSVC consistently performed poorly compared to both.
assertions.anchor: Section 4, RQ1 and Table 2, p.12
quotes: each containing training data instances numbering approximately between 350 and 500
Across the remaining subject systems outlined in the table, QSVC consistently either matches or closely rivals SVC's performance.
Conversely, PQSVC consistently performs poorly compared to both SVC and QSVC across all test scenarios.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on small software-defect datasets, run in simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is a tie with a classical baseline on small datasets, not an advantage; the per-project values sit in Table 2 only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the scalability of QSVC is a significant limitation because of exponential runtime requirements on large datasets, and that they encountered significant challenges in training QSVC with datasets of more than 500 instances.
assertions.anchor: Section 3 (RQ3) p.10 and Section 5 Threats to validity, p.17
quotes: The scalability of QSVC algorithm is a significant limitation due to its exponential runtime requirements when processing large datasets.
we encountered significant challenges in training QSVC with datasets containing more than 500 instances, primarily due to its sluggish runtime.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their own method and experiments in Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results suggest QSVC can offer comparable effectiveness to classical machine learning algorithms in detecting buggy commits under specific conditions, and that the observed performance margin between quantum and classical methods remains modest.
assertions.anchor: Section 7 Conclusion and future work, p.18
quotes: QSVC can offer comparable effectiveness to classical ML algorithms in detecting buggy commits under specific conditions.
However, the observed performance margin between quantum and classical methods remains modest.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own summary of an empirical result from one study.

papers.title_in_file: BCQQ: Batch-Constraint Quantum Q-Learning with Cyclic Data Re-uploading
papers.version_note: The file is arXiv 2305.00905 version 2 (18 Mar 2024), filed under a 2023 folder name; the title and content match the record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, BCQ background, results and discussion (Sections V A, V B part, hardware tests) and conclusion; the effective-dimension derivation was skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: A batch reinforcement learning method that uses variational quantum circuits with cyclic data re-uploading inside discrete batch-constraint Q-learning, tested on CartPole in simulation and on IBM hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum agent with cyclic data re-uploading learned an optimal policy for all buffer sizes, even from just 100 random interactions, in experiments run on a quantum simulator.
assertions.anchor: Section V A, Table I, p.5-6
quotes: the quantum agent with cyclic data re-uploading strategy is able to learn an optimal policy for all buffer sizes, even from just 100 random interactions.
All experiments were performed on a quantum simulator with Qiskit API [44].
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on one low-complexity environment, averaged over three runs.

assertions.value: The authors report that the classical agent trained with discrete BCQ had difficulty learning an optimal policy from small random buffers, that even the larger network could not converge when the buffer was reduced, and they conclude the results indicate BCQQ may show better generalization when learning from smaller data.
assertions.anchor: Section V A (Table I), p.6, and Section VI Conclusion, p.8
quotes: the classical agent trained with discrete BCQ has difficulty learning an optimal policy from small buffers generated using a random policy.
even the larger network was unable to converge to an optimal solution when the size of the training buffer was reduced.
The results also indicate that the BCQQ algorithm may show better generalization and learning capabilities when learning from smaller data compared to classical networks.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical comparison from one study; the authors hedge with 'may'. Parameter counts differ greatly between the two models (Table I only).
assertions.reader_inference: The classical baselines were two fully connected networks with a fixed architecture, so the margin may depend on that choice of baseline.

assertions.value: The authors report that on IBMQ hardware the agent achieved a reward of 90 at the most because of noise, and a reward of 495 with zero noise extrapolation and 1024 shots.
assertions.anchor: Section V, hardware validation (Figure 7), p.8
quotes: The validation results on the IBMQ device show that the agent was only able to achieve a reward of 90 at the most due to the significant impact of noise.
the agent was able to achieve a high reward of 495 with the aid of the zero noise extrapolation error mitigation technique [45] and 1024 shots.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical hardware result from one study; the agent was trained on an ideal simulator and only validated on hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that the limited number of qubits, the hardware topology and the complexity of numerical simulations make it intractable to benchmark quantum reinforcement learning algorithms on state-of-the-art environments on a large scale, and that scaling to more complex circuits and challenging environments is future work.
assertions.anchor: Section I Introduction, p.1, and Section VI Conclusion, p.8
quotes: Currently, the limited number of qubits together with the corresponding hardware topology and the complexity of numerical simulations make it intractable to benchmark QRL algorithms on state-of-the-art environments on a large scale.
For future work, we want to investigate how discrete BCQQ scales with more complex VQCs and evaluate its performance in challenging environments.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their own experiments in Section I and Section VI.
